bib.title: REST: Stress Testing Large Reasoning Models by Asking Multiple Problems at Once

legacy_report:
COVERAGE: 29 of 29 pages (90,371 chars) extracted. Read pp.1-11 (body), appendix A-G (pp.17-20) and the Tab. 6 start. Skimmed: the reference list and the remaining per-stress-level tables (Tab. 6-8, pp.20-29) and error-case figures 14-18. The note's "Lessons" section was skimmed only for its heading and bullet style.

SOURCE: "REST: Stress Testing Large Reasoning Models by Asking Multiple Problems at Once". First author Zhuoshi Pan (equal contribution with Qizhi Pei). Affiliations: Tsinghua University; OpenDataLab, Shanghai AI Laboratory; Renmin University of China. Corresponding authors: H. Vicky Zhao, Conghui He, Lijun Wu. arXiv 2507.10541v2, cs.CL, dated July 16, 2025 (footer says 15 Jul 2025). No venue stated, so preprint. Code: github.com/opendatalab/REST.

CORE CLAIM: Benchmarks near ceiling can be revived without writing new questions. Concatenate s consecutive questions into one prompt ("stress level" s, cyclic indexing, prompt-set size stays N). Accuracy then falls sharply for many reasoning models, and models that tie on single-question scores separate.

HEADLINE NUMBERS (all: Tab. 1, 34 LRMs from 1.5B to 671B, 32K max output tokens, OpenCompass, rule-based \boxed{} extraction; "Stress" = mean accuracy over stress levels >1; AIME24, AIME25 and AMC23 averaged over 8 sampling runs)
1. DeepSeek-R1 on AIME24: single 81.66, stress 52.49. The text gives the drop as 29.17%; the AIME25 drop is 31.58% (68.75 to 37.17). Stress levels s in {2..5}.
2. Discrimination on MATH500, stress levels {3,5,7,9}: R1-Distill-Qwen-7B single 93.0, stress 66.75. R1-Distill-Qwen-32B single 94.6, stress 88.97. A 1.6-point single gap becomes a 22.22-point gap.
3. Post-training does not carry over. AReaL-boba-RL-7B scores 95.0 single and 60.77 stress on MATH500. OpenThinker2-7B scores 93.8 and 83.30. Base R1-7B scores 93.0 and 66.75, so both Light-R1-7B-DS (61.73) and AReaL fall below it. At s=9 they get 38.07 and 39.11 against R1-7B's 49.42.
4. Ranking flips. R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B beats Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B-Inst on MATH500 single (83.40 vs 73.00). Under stress it loses (42.47 vs 53.94).
5. Long2Short helps. Efficient-R1-7B (α=0.2) has lower single accuracy than R1-7B (88.20 vs 93.00) but reaches 66.02 vs 49.42 at s=9 on MATH500, a 16.60 margin. L1-Qwen-1.5B-Max beats R1-1.5B by 44.71 points at s=9.
Also: easy tasks barely move. GSM8K drops are 0.43% for R1-7B and 0.04% for R1-32B (text). Lengthening the output limit from 32K to 128K changes almost nothing (R1-7B AIME24 16.53 to 16.17, Tab. 5).

QUOTES
- "Even state-of-the-art (SOTA) models like DeepSeek-R1 exhibit substantial performance degradation under stress testing, challenging the prevailing assumption that 'LLMs are multi-problem solvers'." (p.1)
- "REST ... significantly amplifies performance differences among models that exhibit comparable, near-ceiling accuracy in traditional single-question evaluations." (p.6)

MECHANISMS: Error analysis on AIME24 (Fig. 5). Question Omission and Reasoning Error together account for 42.00% of DeepSeek-R1's degradation. For Light-R1-7B, Endless Repetition plus Output Truncation account for 48.90%. No format violations were found for the four models analysed, which supports the extraction design. Accuracy falls with question position (Fig. 7). Easy-first ordering beats hard-first (Fig. 8). Models that do well use fewer reasoning tokens on the first question (Fig. 6).

LIMITS
- The authors concede two limits (App. E): higher evaluation cost (longer reasoning) and that newer models may be missing; they plan a leaderboard.
- Only reasoning models were run on math, GPQA and LiveCodeBench; non-reasoning models were run only as comparisons.
- It does not show that stress scores predict real multi-issue deployment quality. The tutoring and support cases are motivation only.
- It does not test contamination directly. The abstract cites contamination, but there is no contamination experiment.
- Position and difficulty effects are confounded. Difficulty order uses R1-7B's fail rate as the proxy.
- Rule-based extraction understates accuracy (App. C): R1-7B MATH500 is 66.75 rule-based vs 70.59 with a gemma-3-27b-it extractor.
- Stress levels were chosen per benchmark, so scores are not comparable across benchmarks.
- Models are from early to mid 2025 and have dated.

BUILDS ON: Batch prompting (Cheng et al. [6]), multi-problem prompting [54] and multi-task inference benchmark [44]. These tested only simple tasks such as text classification. Also MathFusion [36] and Mosaic-IT [24] (problem concatenation for training data), Compound-QA [19], overthinking [45, 5, 53], and Long2Short methods (L1 [1], Efficient-R1 [3]). Benchmarks reused: GSM8K, MATH500, AMC23, AIME24, AIME25, GPQA Diamond, LiveCodeBench v5.

BEST-FIT SECTION: "Lessons from public benchmarks" in /Users/ramsey-wise/workspace/learn-ai-engineering/generative-ai/08-eval/notes/03-eval-datasets.md. Suggested bullet: a saturated set can be made harder and more discriminating by composing rows, but score the compositions at several stress levels. Alternative: the "Contamination" subsection (line 283), as a way to refresh a leaked set cheaply. Not a fit for "Row eligibility". Caveat: the paper makes no contamination test, so cite it as saturation and discrimination only.

FIGURE CANDIDATE: Fig. 1 (p.2), single vs stress accuracy per model on MATH500. It shows the 1.6-point vs 22.22-point gap at a glance. Runner-up: Fig. 2 (p.7), accuracy against questions per input.

PROBLEMS: None. The extraction is clean apart from figure and table text, which is flattened. The PDF has no embedded instructions.
